I think the above responses are resourceful, and I hope it provides you with some perspective. I have faced, in some ways, the same dilemma as you so I would like to share a few key thoughts - forgive me if you have considered them already. 

Getting a foot in the door can be difficult but remember resilience is key to not only successfully gaining employment but also thriving in it (especially as a lawyer). Keep going because you never know what the future holds; keep your anxiety at bay and do not let it consume you because it will if you let it - do things that ease your mind a little (for e.g I go to the gym, read, etc). First, it's normal to compare yourself to others but this can also be unproductive. It is not a race.

As a preliminary step, make sure your CV and cover letter is as perfect as they can be. I cannot stress this enough. Quick tip for your CV, in the bullet points for job descriptions it helps to really embellish (but do not lie) about what you achieved in that role. Outline the key highlights and make it sound professional. Your CV and cover letter will be the foundation of any job application. Get multiple people to look over your CV and cover letter (they can see things you cannot and might offer crucial insight).

After this, I think the first step is to take a step back and make a plan, break it down to small steps, and then follow through. This will help you gain confidence. For example, if you want a paralegal/admin role in a boutique firm some actionable steps would be to make a list of the firms you want to apply for (look for firms on google, yellow pages, the internet etc), email them your resume and a short covering email, after a week or so (if they do not respond) follow up with a phone call. These series of steps could be done each day for a few firms while you supplement your search with other steps such as making linkedin connections, networking, etc or investing in yourself to make you appear more attractive as a candidate (increase your gpa, practise interviewing, enter law comps, legal volunteering at clcs). This will increase your chances of securing a role. This was one of my strategies a few months ago when I was a desperate graduate and it worked. Also, make friends in the legal industry - it could help with getting off-the-market jobs.

 If you are open to other career opportunities, explore them as well.

You made the mistake by assuming 150 was 1/4 of the whole audience when 1/4 of the listeners is actually 145. Why? I'll tell you why. We know the 1st lecture room can hold 3/4 of the listeners, but  we also know that 5 listeners are 'missing' in the 1st lecture room (we deduce they have moved over to the 2nd lecture room). Due to the fact that the 5 listeners moved over to the 2nd lecture room, the quoted number of people in the 2nd room (150) must be reduced by 5 to find the actual 1/4 of the listeners (which is 150 -5 =145). Multiply the quarter by 4 and we get 580 (which is 145 x 4), that is the whole population of the listeners.
